stem: A 43-year-old woman at 10 weeks' gestation has first-trimester screening. Ultrasound shows a nuchal translucency of 4.2 mm (thickened). Serum PAPP-A is 0.3 MoM (low) and free β-hCG is 2.6 MoM (high).
oneliner: 43F + 10 wk + thick nuchal translucency + low PAPP-A + high β-hCG → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **β-hCG is low** in trisomy 18; here it is high
whyNot.C: **β-hCG low or normal** with very low PAPP-A; the high β-hCG here does not fit
whyNot.D: Raises **AFP**; does not give a thick nuchal translucency with high β-hCG
whyNot.E: **Screening markers are normal**; no thick nuchal translucency or hormone shift

why: **Thick nuchal translucency + low PAPP-A + high β-hCG** in an older mother = trisomy 21.

stem: A newborn girl has upslanting palpebral fissures, a single palmar crease and hypotonia. Her karyotype shows 46 chromosomes, with extra chromosome 21 material attached to chromosome 14 in every cell. Her healthy mother has 45 chromosomes with a 14;21 fusion.
oneliner: Newborn F + Down features + 46 chromosomes, extra 21 attached to 14 + mother has 45 chromosomes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Down syndrome from a Robertsonian translocation

whyNot.A: Gives **47 chromosomes with a free extra 21**; here there are 46 and a 14;21 fusion
whyNot.B: Needs **a mix of normal and trisomic cells**; here every cell carries the translocation
whyNot.C: Would show **extra chromosome 18**, clenched fists and rocker-bottom feet
whyNot.E: Would be **45,X**, with neck webbing; the karyotype here has an extra 21 segment

why: **46 chromosomes with 21 fused to 14**, and a carrier mother with **45 chromosomes** = Robertsonian translocation Down syndrome.

stem: A stillborn boy has a single central eye, a midline cleft lip and palate, and an extra finger on each hand.
oneliner: Stillborn M + single central eye + cleft lip and palate + extra fingers → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has **clenched overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet**, not cyclopia or clefts
whyNot.C: **Flat face and upslanting eyes**; no midline brain or eye defect
whyNot.D: **Cystic hygroma and lymphedema**; no cyclopia or polydactyly
whyNot.E: May have a palate defect but **no cyclopia or polydactyly**

why: **Cyclopia (holoprosencephaly) + midline clefts + polydactyly** = trisomy 13.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has never had a period. She is 140 cm tall (below the 3rd percentile) and has minimal breast and pubic hair development. Serum FSH is markedly elevated.
oneliner: 16F + never menstruated + 140 cm + little breast/pubic hair + high FSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Constitutional delay of growth and puberty

whyNot.A: **FSH is low** (prepubertal) in a late bloomer; here it is high
whyNot.B: **FSH and LH are low**; the ovaries would not be failing
whyNot.C: Has **normal breast development** and is usually tall
whyNot.D: **Low FSH** with loss of smell, and normal height

why: **Short stature + absent puberty + high FSH** = ovarian failure from gonadal dysgenesis (Turner syndrome).

stem: A 15-year-old girl is short, has a broad chest and has never menstruated. Pelvic ultrasound shows a small uterus and no visible ovaries. Karyotype from blood shows 45,X in some cells and 46,XX in the others.
oneliner: 15F + short + broad chest + primary amenorrhea + blood cells part 45,X part 46,XX → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Is **47,XXY in a male** with small testes
whyNot.B: Has a **46,XY karyotype** with a normal-sized uterus
whyNot.D: Has a **normal karyotype**, with pulmonary stenosis and normal ovarian function
whyNot.E: Needs **a Y-bearing cell line (46,XX/46,XY)**; no Y here

why: **Short stature + streak ovaries + a mix of 45,X and 46,XX cells** = mosaic Turner syndrome.

stem: A newborn girl has a large soft swelling at the back of the neck, puffy swollen feet, and a narrow aorta (coarctation) on echocardiogram.
oneliner: Newborn F + cystic hygroma + puffy feet + coarctation of aorta → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Typically has **an atrioventricular septal defect**, flat face and hypotonia
whyNot.C: Typical lesion is **pulmonary valve stenosis** with a normal karyotype
whyNot.D: Has **clenched fists, rocker-bottom feet** and a small jaw
whyNot.E: Occurs in **boys** and is not recognised at birth

why: **Cystic hygroma + lymphedema of the feet + coarctation** in a girl = 45,X.

stem: A 28-year-old man is evaluated for infertility. Semen analysis shows azoospermia and his testes are small and firm. A testicular biopsy specimen is shown.
oneliner: 28M + infertility + azoospermia + small firm testes + [biopsy] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Testes are **normal in size** and fertility is usually preserved
whyNot.B: Patients have a **female phenotype**; this is a man
whyNot.C: Small soft testes with **arrested maturation and low gonadotropins**, not scarred tubules
whyNot.D: Tubules contain **Sertoli cells without germ cells**, not hyalinized tubules with Leydig clusters

why: **Hyalinized seminiferous tubules + Leydig cell clusters** with small firm testes = Klinefelter syndrome.

image.prompt: H&E photomicrograph of a testicular biopsy: shrunken seminiferous tubules with thick, pink, glassy hyalinized walls and no germ cells, separated by prominent clusters of pale Leydig cells.

stem: A 2-day-old boy is cyanotic and has a seizure. Echocardiogram shows tetralogy of Fallot. Serum calcium is 6.2 mg/dL and lymphocyte count is low; the chest x-ray shows no thymic shadow. Routine G-banded karyotype is 46,XY.
oneliner: 2d M + cyanosis + tetralogy of Fallot + low calcium + low lymphocytes + normal karyotype → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Karyotype would show **an extra chromosome 21**; heart lesion is usually AV canal
whyNot.B: Occurs in **girls** with coarctation and a 45,X karyotype
whyNot.D: Has **hypercalcemia** and supravalvular aortic stenosis
whyNot.E: Karyotype would show **an extra chromosome 18**, with clenched fists

why: **Conotruncal heart defect + hypocalcemia + low T cells with absent thymus** and a normal routine karyotype = 22q11.2 microdeletion.

stem: A 36-year-old woman has chorionic villus sampling at 11 weeks. About 40% of cells in several separate villus samples show trisomy 15; the rest are 46,XY. Amniocentesis at 16 weeks shows 46,XY in all cells, and ultrasound is normal.
oneliner: 36F + CVS: trisomy 15 in some cells of several samples + amniocentesis 46,XY + normal ultrasound → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **Fetal (amniotic) cells would also carry the abnormal line**; they are all normal here
whyNot.C: Abnormal cells appear in **a single culture or colony**, not in several independent samples
whyNot.D: Would add **46,XX cells**; the villus sample here is 46,XY
whyNot.E: **All fetal cells would be trisomic** and the pregnancy usually fails

why: **Trisomy 15 only in placental tissue** with a **normal amniotic fluid karyotype** = confined placental mosaicism.

stem: A 17-year-old girl, 175 cm tall with a BMI of 22, has never menstruated. Exam shows normal breast development, almost no pubic or axillary hair, and a vagina that ends blindly. Pelvic ultrasound shows no uterus.
oneliner: 17F + primary amenorrhea + normal breasts + no pubic/axillary hair + blind vagina → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has **normal pubic and axillary hair** because ovaries and adrenals are normal
whyNot.B: **Short stature** with little breast development
whyNot.C: Uterus is present and **BMI is low**
whyNot.E: Uterus, vagina and **pubic hair are normal**; periods usually occur

why: **Breasts present, no pubic/axillary hair, blind vagina, no uterus** = 46,XY with androgen receptor defect.

stem: A newborn has normal-appearing female external genitalia. Prenatal karyotype was 46,XY. Ultrasound shows no uterus or fallopian tubes, and testes are palpable in the labia. Serum testosterone and dihydrotestosterone are both in the normal male range.
oneliner: Newborn + female-appearing genitalia + 46,XY + no uterus + testes + normal testosterone and DHT → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **DHT is low** with ambiguous genitalia; here DHT is normal
whyNot.B: Has **a uterus and streak gonads** with low testosterone
whyNot.D: Is **46,XX with ovaries**, not testes
whyNot.E: Virilizes a **46,XX** infant that has a uterus and ovaries

why: **46,XY with testes and normal testosterone/DHT but female genitalia and no uterus** = androgen receptor resistance.

stem: A 6-month-old girl has bilateral inguinal hernias. At repair, the surgeon finds a gonad in each sac and biopsy shows testicular tissue. The vagina is short and blind, no uterus is seen, and serum testosterone, dihydrotestosterone and LH are all high.
oneliner: 6mo F + bilateral inguinal hernias + testes in the sacs + blind vagina + no uterus + high testosterone, DHT and LH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **DHT is low**, with ambiguous genitalia; DHT is high here
whyNot.C: Affects **46,XX infants with ovaries and a uterus**
whyNot.D: Has **streak gonads and a uterus**, with low testosterone
whyNot.E: Has **ovaries, not testes**, and normal hormones

why: **Testes in hernia sacs + female genitalia + no uterus + high testosterone and LH** = end-organ resistance to androgens.

stem: A newborn has normal male external genitalia with both testes descended. Amniocentesis earlier in pregnancy showed a 46,XX karyotype. Ultrasound shows no uterus or fallopian tubes.
oneliner: Newborn + normal male genitalia + testes + prenatal karyotype 46,XX + no uterus → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: A 46,XX infant would have **ovaries, a uterus and virilized female genitalia**
whyNot.B: Is **46,XY** with female external genitalia
whyNot.C: Karyotype is **47,XXY**, and it is not detected at birth
whyNot.E: Is 46,XY with a female phenotype and **streak gonads**

answer: 46,XX testicular disorder of sex development (SRY translocation)
why: **46,XX karyotype with normal testes and male genitalia** = SRY gene translocated onto the X chromosome.

stem: A 2-month-old girl, recently adopted, feeds slowly and tires during bottle feeding. A photograph of her face is shown.
oneliner: 2mo F + slow feeding + [photo of face] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: The **upper lip would be intact**; the photo shows a lip defect
whyNot.C: Has a **small receded jaw**; the jaw here looks normal
whyNot.D: Shows **underdeveloped ear and jaw on one side**, not a lip gap
whyNot.E: Causes **drooping and loss of movement**, not a split in the lip

stem: A healthy-appearing newborn boy has a left-sided cleft lip and palate with a normal-sized jaw, no lip pits and no other malformations. Parents are unrelated and nobody in the family has a similar defect.
oneliner: Newborn M + unilateral cleft lip and palate + normal jaw + no other anomalies + no family history → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has **midline brain, eye and limb defects** such as polydactyly, not an isolated cleft
whyNot.B: Has **a small jaw** with the tongue falling back
whyNot.C: Has **hypoplastic jaw, cheekbones and ears**
whyNot.D: Has **lower-lip pits** and an autosomal dominant family history

stem: A newborn girl has a small jaw, underdeveloped cheekbones, downslanting eyes and malformed ears on both sides. She fails her hearing screen (conductive loss).
oneliner: Newborn F + small jaw + hypoplastic cheekbones + malformed ears + conductive hearing loss → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has a small jaw with **cleft palate and tongue displacement**; cheekbones and ears are normal
whyNot.B: Has **heart defects, low calcium and thymic hypoplasia**
whyNot.C: Is typically **one-sided** and may show vertebral anomalies
whyNot.E: Has **premature skull-suture fusion** with bulging eyes

why: **Symmetric hypoplasia of jaw, cheekbones and ears with conductive deafness** = first pharyngeal arch (neural crest) defect.

stem: A term newborn boy has severe respiratory distress and no urine output from birth. Pregnancy had severe oligohydramnios. He dies within hours; autopsy shows absent kidneys, small lungs and an intact diaphragm.
oneliner: Term newborn M + severe oligohydramnios + no urine + small lungs + absent kidneys → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has a **diaphragmatic defect with bowel in the chest** and normal kidneys
whyNot.C: Affects **preterm infants with hyaline membranes** and normal-sized lungs
whyNot.D: Shows **enlarged cystic kidneys**, not absent ones
whyNot.E: Has **meconium-stained fluid** and normal kidneys

why: **Absent kidneys + oligohydramnios + pulmonary hypoplasia** = Potter sequence.

stem: A newborn boy has a flattened nose, low-set ears with a skin fold below each eye, and bilateral clubfeet. Prenatal ultrasound showed too little amniotic fluid. He has respiratory distress, and imaging shows small, cystic dysplastic kidneys.
oneliner: Newborn M + flat face + clubfeet + low amniotic fluid + cystic dysplastic kidneys → ?

whyNot.A: **Upslanting eyes, hypotonia and AV canal**; clubfeet and low fluid are not typical
whyNot.B: Has **clenched overlapping fingers and rocker-bottom feet**, with excess amniotic fluid
whyNot.C: Occurs in **girls** with cystic hygroma and horseshoe kidney
whyNot.D: Has **cleft lip, polydactyly and brain malformation**

stem: A newborn boy has cataracts, a patent ductus arteriosus murmur and failed hearing screen. His mother had a rash with swollen occipital lymph nodes in the first trimester. Head CT shows no intracranial calcification.
oneliner: Newborn M + cataracts + PDA + deafness + maternal 1st-trimester rash and occipital nodes → ?

whyNot.A: Shows **periventricular calcification**, which is absent here; cataract and PDA are not typical

stem: A 14-year-old boy of normal weight has intellectual disability and speech delay. He has a long narrow face with a prominent jaw, large ears, hyperextensible finger joints and testes that are larger than expected for his age. His mother's brother has a similar disability.
oneliner: 14M + intellectual disability + long face + large ears + big testes + affected maternal uncle → ?

whyNot.B: Has **small firm testes** and tall stature
whyNot.C: Shows **upslanting eyes, flat face and normal-sized testes**
whyNot.D: Has **obesity, hyperphagia and small genitalia**
whyNot.E: Affects **girls** with loss of hand skills and hand-wringing

why: **Long face + large ears + macro-orchidism + X-linked family pattern** = FMR1 CGG repeat expansion.

stem: A 4-year-old boy has delayed speech, hand-flapping and poor eye contact. His head is large and his ears are prominent. His mother's brother has intellectual disability.
oneliner: 4M + delayed speech + hand-flapping + large head and ears + maternal uncle with intellectual disability → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Would not explain **macrocephaly, large ears or the X-linked family history**
whyNot.B: Has **upslanting eyes, flat face and hypotonia**

stem: A 30-year-old woman's brother has intellectual disability and enlarged testes. Her 5-year-old son and 3-year-old daughter both have mild developmental delay and prominent ears.
oneliner: 30F + brother with intellectual disability and big testes + son and daughter with mild delay and large ears → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.D: Affects **girls only**, with regression and hand-wringing
whyNot.E: Is **not familial** and does not cause macro-orchidism

why: **X-linked family with intellectual disability, big testes and large ears; both sexes affected in the next generation** = Fragile X.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has obesity with constant hunger, intellectual disability, small genitalia and a history of severe hypotonia in infancy. FISH for a 15q11-q13 deletion is normal, and methylation testing shows only the maternal pattern on chromosome 15.

whyNot.E: Is **overgrowth with macroglossia**, not obesity from hunger

stem: A 2-year-old boy is above the 97th percentile for height and weight and has a large tongue. He had an omphalocele repaired at birth. A flank mass is found, and biopsy shows blastemal, epithelial and stromal cells.

stem: A 7-year-old girl has had multiple skin lesions since early childhood and now has freckling in both armpits. A photograph of her back is shown.

stem: A 27-year-old man is diagnosed with a soft tissue sarcoma. His mother had breast cancer at 33, his brother died of a brain tumor at 19, and his aunt had adrenocortical carcinoma in childhood.

stem: A newborn boy has no visible iris in either eye. His father has the same finding. Both have normal development and normal kidneys on ultrasound; karyotypes show a balanced translocation with a breakpoint near 11p13 and no missing material.

stem: A newborn girl has a white forelock and fails her newborn hearing screen with sensorineural loss. Her mother also has a white forelock and is deaf in one ear.

stem: A 16-year-old boy is 190 cm tall with long thin fingers and a long narrow face. The lenses of both eyes are displaced upward. Echocardiogram shows a dilated aortic root and mitral valve prolapse. His father, also tall, died of aortic dissection at 41. Intelligence is normal.

stem: A 12-year-old boy and his older brother have each had more than 15 fractures after minor falls. Both have blue-gray sclerae and hearing loss, and the fractures healed normally. Neither boy has had unexplained bruising, and child-protection review found nothing suspicious.

stem: A 4-month-old boy has lost the ability to hold up his head and now has seizures. His hair is sparse, kinky and pale. Serum copper and ceruloplasmin are both low. A maternal uncle died in infancy with similar illness.

stem: A 5-year-old boy falls often and must push on his thighs to stand up from the floor. His calves look enlarged.

whyNot.B: Is **milder and later**; the uncle lost walking at 10 and died at 19

whyNot.D: Shows **fasciculations, absent reflexes and neurogenic EMG** with normal CK
whyNot.E: Gives **ascending weakness with slowed nerve conduction**, and normal CK

why: **Proximal myopathy + calf pseudohypertrophy + very high CK + X-linked pattern** = DMD (frameshift dystrophin deletion).

stem: An 11-year-old boy has a chronic productive cough, repeated sinus infections, nasal polyps and finger clubbing. Sputum cultures grow Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Sweat chloride is 88 mEq/L (normal under 30).
oneliner: 11M + chronic productive cough + sinus infections + nasal polyps + clubbing + Pseudomonas + sweat chloride 88 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has **normal sweat chloride** and often situs inversus
whyNot.B: Gives **reversible wheeze without clubbing or Pseudomonas**
whyNot.C: Is **intestinal** and gives no chronic lung infection
whyNot.E: Has **neutropenia and pancreatic insufficiency** with normal sweat chloride

why: **Chronic Pseudomonas lung disease + polyps + clubbing + high sweat chloride** = CFTR defect.

stem: A 16-year-old girl has chronic lung infection with Pseudomonas and bulky greasy stools. Genetic testing shows she is homozygous for a 3-base-pair deletion that removes phenylalanine at position 508 of a protein encoded on chromosome 7. The protein is made but misfolds and is degraded.
oneliner: 16F + chronic Pseudomonas lung infection + greasy stools + homozygous ΔF508 on chromosome 7 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Comes from **dynein arm defects** on other chromosomes, with normal sweat chloride
whyNot.C: Involves **chromosome 14** with emphysema and liver disease
whyNot.D: Has **neutropenia and skeletal changes** (SBDS gene)
whyNot.E: Causes **recurrent pancreatitis** without chronic lung infection

why: **ΔF508 on chromosome 7 with lung infection and pancreatic insufficiency** = CFTR misfolding and degradation.

stem: An 18-month-old girl has had four episodes of pneumonia and passes bulky, greasy stools. Her weight is below the 3rd percentile. Sweat chloride is 82 mEq/L. Her parents are healthy and her older brother has the same illness.
oneliner: 18mo F + 4 pneumonias + greasy stools + poor growth + sweat chloride 82 + healthy parents, affected brother → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Causes **diarrhea and poor growth after gluten** but not recurrent pneumonia, and sweat chloride is normal
whyNot.B: Has **normal sweat chloride** and no fat malabsorption
whyNot.C: Affects **boys only** with infections but **no steatorrhea** and a normal sweat test
whyNot.D: Has **neutropenia and skeletal changes** with normal sweat chloride

why: **Recurrent pneumonia + steatorrhea + high sweat chloride with healthy parents and an affected sibling** = autosomal recessive CF.

stem: A 9-year-old boy has had greasy stools since infancy, recurrent chest infections, a chronic cough and poor weight gain. He now has an unsteady gait, absent ankle reflexes and loss of position sense in his feet. Blood smear shows normal red cells, and cholesterol and triglycerides are normal.
oneliner: 9M + greasy stools since infancy + recurrent chest infections + poor growth + new ataxia, absent reflexes, lost position sense + normal smear and lipids → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Shows **acanthocytes and very low cholesterol and triglycerides**, without chest infections
whyNot.B: Does not cause **recurrent chest infections** and has gluten-related symptoms
whyNot.C: Has **cardiomyopathy and kyphoscoliosis** with no fat malabsorption or lung disease
whyNot.E: Gives chronic chest and sinus disease but **no steatorrhea**

why: **Steatorrhea + recurrent chest infections + failure to thrive** = CF; the **ataxia and areflexia** come from fat-soluble vitamin E malabsorption.

stem: A 3-week-old boy has an elevated immunoreactive trypsinogen on newborn screening. Sweat chloride is 72 mEq/L on two separate tests. A CFTR panel finds only one known disease-causing mutation. He is feeding well and has no cough.
oneliner: 3wk M + high newborn-screen trypsinogen + sweat chloride 72 twice + only one CFTR mutation found → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Carriers have **normal sweat chloride**
whyNot.C: Has **intermediate sweat chloride (30-59 mEq/L)**, not a repeated value above 60
whyNot.D: Has **normal sweat chloride**
whyNot.E: Has **neutropenia** and a normal sweat test

why: **Repeated sweat chloride over 60 mEq/L** is diagnostic of CF even when only one CFTR mutation is found.

stem: A 29-year-old woman has chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis and one tubal ectopic pregnancy. Her husband's semen analysis is normal. Sweat chloride and serum immunoglobulin levels are normal.
oneliner: 29F + chronic sinusitis + bronchiectasis + tubal ectopic pregnancy + normal sweat chloride + normal immunoglobulins → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has a **high sweat chloride** and pancreatic insufficiency
whyNot.B: Gives **obstructive azoospermia in men**; it does not explain tubal ectopic pregnancy in a woman
whyNot.C: Shows **low immunoglobulins**; levels are normal here
whyNot.D: Causes **basal emphysema and liver disease**, not sinusitis with bronchiectasis

why: **Chronic sinusitis + bronchiectasis + tubal ectopic pregnancy** (poor tubal ciliary transport) with normal sweat chloride and immunoglobulins = primary ciliary dyskinesia (dynein arm defect).

stem: A 38-year-old man has never smoked but has progressive exertional dyspnea and wheezing. His father died of lung and liver disease at 46. Exam shows a hyperinflated chest and a palpable liver edge. Spirometry shows an FEV1/FVC of 0.55 and FEV1 48% of predicted with little response to bronchodilator; TLC is increased and DLCO is reduced. CT shows emphysema that is worst at the lung bases. ALT is mildly elevated.
oneliner: 38M nonsmoker + dyspnea + wheeze + hepatomegaly + basal emphysema + low DLCO + father died of lung and liver disease at 46 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Is **upper-lobe emphysema** in a smoker, and does not give liver disease
whyNot.B: Has **reversible obstruction with normal DLCO**
whyNot.D: Has **bronchiectasis and a high sweat chloride**, with upper-lobe predominance
whyNot.E: Is defined by **productive cough for months** and does not cause basal emphysema or liver disease

why: **Young nonsmoker + basal panacinar emphysema + liver involvement + family history** = alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency.

stem: A 48-year-old man has bronze skin, pain in the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints, and an enlarged liver. His brother has cirrhosis. Serum ferritin is 1,200 ng/mL (normal 24-336) and transferrin saturation is 80% (normal 20-50%).
oneliner: 48M + bronze skin + 2nd/3rd MCP arthropathy + hepatomegaly + ferritin 1,200 + transferrin saturation 80% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Gives **low ceruloplasmin, Kayser-Fleischer rings** and presents younger
whyNot.C: Does not cause **bronze skin or high transferrin saturation**
whyNot.D: Causes **blistering photosensitive lesions on the hands**
whyNot.E: Has **hypotension and low cortisol**, with normal iron studies

why: **Bronze skin + MCP arthropathy + liver disease + transferrin saturation 80%** = HFE-related iron overload.

stem: A 45-year-old man has heart failure with a dilated left ventricle, and a random glucose of 320 mg/dL. His father and uncle died of cardiomyopathy in their forties. An endomyocardial biopsy stained with Prussian blue is shown.
oneliner: 45M + dilated cardiomyopathy + glucose 320 + father and uncle died young of cardiomyopathy + [Prussian blue biopsy] → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Shows **apple-green birefringence with Congo red**, with restrictive physiology
whyNot.B: Causes **liver and basal ganglia disease** and copper, not iron, deposits
whyNot.C: Shows **eosinophil infiltrate** on biopsy
whyNot.D: Shows **vacuolated glycogen-filled myocytes** and presents in infancy

why: **Iron granules in cardiac myocytes + diabetes + familial cardiomyopathy** = iron-overload cardiomyopathy.

image.prompt: Photomicrograph of heart muscle (endomyocardial biopsy) stained with Prussian blue: cardiac myocytes contain many coarse blue granules of iron in the cytoplasm, around the nuclei.

stem: A 16-year-old boy has a coarse "wing-beating" tremor of the arms and a greenish-brown ring at the edge of each cornea. Serum ceruloplasmin is low.
oneliner: 16M + wing-beating tremor + greenish-brown corneal rings + low ceruloplasmin → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Is **iron overload with bronze skin and high ferritin**, with normal ceruloplasmin
whyNot.B: Does not occur at 16 and has **no corneal rings**
whyNot.D: Causes **emphysema and liver disease**, with no corneal rings or tremor
whyNot.E: Gives **jaundice and positive serology**, not corneal rings or tremor

why: **Kayser-Fleischer rings + tremor + low ceruloplasmin** in a teenager = ATP7B copper overload.

stem: A 7-month-old boy, adopted from abroad with no birth records, has seizures and has lost previously gained milestones. He has fair skin and blond hair, though his parents are dark-haired, and his urine smells musty.
oneliner: 7mo M + seizures + developmental delay + fair skin and blond hair + musty urine odor → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Gives a **maple syrup odor** with poor feeding and ketoacidosis
whyNot.C: Has **lens dislocation and thrombosis**, with a marfanoid body
whyNot.D: Gives a **cabbage-like odor with liver failure**
whyNot.E: Has **nystagmus and translucent irises** but normal development and no odor

why: **Musty odor + fair hair and skin + seizures and delay** = phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency.

stem: A 5-day-old boy is well, but newborn screening shows a serum phenylalanine of 22 mg/dL (normal under 2).
oneliner: 5d M + well + newborn screen phenylalanine 22 mg/dL → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Raises **tyrosine and succinylacetone**, not phenylalanine
whyNot.B: Raises **leucine, isoleucine and valine**
whyNot.C: Raises **methionine and homocysteine**
whyNot.E: Raises **galactose-1-phosphate** and causes jaundice, cataracts and sepsis

why: **Markedly high phenylalanine on newborn screen** = phenylalanine hydroxylase (or BH4 cofactor) deficiency.

stem: A 6-month-old boy born at home has no newborn screening. He has eczema, microcephaly, fair hair and developmental delay. Plasma phenylalanine is 25 mg/dL (high) and tyrosine is low.
oneliner: 6mo M + eczema + microcephaly + fair hair + delay + high phenylalanine and low tyrosine → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Has **high tyrosine** with liver failure and renal tubular disease
whyNot.C: Has **high branched-chain amino acids** and a sweet odor
whyNot.D: Has **high methionine and homocysteine** with lens dislocation
whyNot.E: Has **nystagmus and normal amino acids**

why: **High phenylalanine with low tyrosine** (tyrosine becomes essential; less melanin and catecholamines) = PKU.

stem: A 2-month-old girl has white hair, pink-white skin, translucent irises and avoids bright light.
oneliner: 2mo F + white hair + pink skin + translucent irises + photophobia → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Gives **a white forelock and patches** with normal skin elsewhere and normal irises
whyNot.C: Has **deafness, a white forelock and wide-set eyes**
whyNot.D: Gives **silvery hair with recurrent infections** and giant granules
whyNot.E: Causes **acquired white patches**, not diffuse pallor from birth

why: **Diffuse lack of pigment + translucent irises + photophobia** = tyrosinase-related melanin defect.

stem: A 6-year-old Nigerian boy has reddish-bronze skin and ginger-red hair, although both parents have dark skin and black hair. He has nystagmus, reduced visual acuity and partly translucent irises. He does not bruise easily and has no unusual infections. Genetic testing shows two different mutations in the gene for tyrosinase-related protein 1, one inherited from each parent.
oneliner: 6M Nigerian + red-bronze skin + red hair + nystagmus + translucent irises + compound TYRP1 mutations → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Affects **the eyes only**, with normal skin and hair color, and is X-linked
whyNot.B: Gives **acquired depigmented patches**, not diffuse red pigment with nystagmus
whyNot.C: Adds **bleeding and bruising from platelet dysfunction**
whyNot.E: Adds **recurrent infections**, with silvery rather than red hair

why: **Red-bronze skin, red hair, nystagmus and biallelic TYRP1 mutations** = autosomal recessive albinism (OCA3).

stem: A 26-year-old man with normal skin color and his wife, who also has normal pigmentation, are counseled before pregnancy. The man's younger brother was born with white hair, very pale skin, blue-gray irises, nystagmus and marked light sensitivity affecting the whole body. Neither parent of the brothers is affected. No one else in either family is affected, and the couple are unrelated.
oneliner: 26M + brother born with white hair, pale skin, nystagmus, photophobia + unaffected parents + couple unrelated → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Affects **the eyes mainly, with normal skin and hair**
whyNot.C: Is **acquired patchy depigmentation** without nystagmus
whyNot.D: Gives **musty odor and intellectual disability**, with fair hair but normal eyes
whyNot.E: Causes **a white forelock and patches** with normal vision

why: **Whole-body pigment loss with nystagmus and photophobia, unaffected parents** = autosomal recessive OCA; the unaffected sibling has a 2/3 chance of being a carrier.

stem: A 3-year-old girl has progressive stiffness of the legs and dystonic posturing that is worse in the evening and better after sleep. MRI of the brain is normal. CSF homovanillic acid is low, 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid is normal, and CSF lactate and plasma phenylalanine are normal.
oneliner: 3F + leg stiffness + dystonia worse in evening + normal MRI + low CSF HVA, normal 5-HIAA → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Is **static** and is not diurnal; CSF neurotransmitter metabolites are normal
whyNot.B: Has **liver disease, Kayser-Fleischer rings and low ceruloplasmin**
whyNot.D: Has **raised lactate** and structural brain abnormalities
whyNot.E: Gives **low 5-HIAA** with normal HVA

why: **Dystonia with diurnal variation + normal MRI + low HVA but normal 5-HIAA** = failure of dopamine synthesis from tyrosine.

stem: A 7-day-old boy is brought in with poor feeding, vomiting, and increasing lethargy. He is hypotonic, and his urine has a smell like burnt sugar.
oneliner: 7d M + poor feeding + vomiting + lethargy + hypotonia + burnt-sugar urine odor → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **musty or mousy odor**; infants are normal at birth, not encephalopathic in week 1
whyNot.B: **sweaty-feet odor**, not burnt sugar
whyNot.D: **no characteristic urine odor**; would be led by jaundice, hepatomegaly and sepsis
whyNot.E: **presents later** with lens dislocation or thrombosis, not neonatal encephalopathy

why: **Burnt-sugar urine odor** with neonatal lethargy and vomiting = branched-chain alpha-keto acid dehydrogenase deficiency (leucine, isoleucine, valine build up).

stem: A 24-year-old woman is admitted with a deep venous thrombosis of the leg. She has mild intellectual disability, and an eye exam shows both lenses displaced downward. Her parents and siblings are healthy.
oneliner: 24F + DVT + mild intellectual disability + downward lens dislocation + healthy parents → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **upward** lens dislocation, normal intelligence and no thrombosis; lenses here are displaced downward
whyNot.C: **no lens dislocation or thrombosis**; features are ID, musty odor, fair skin
whyNot.D: **liver failure and renal tubular disease**; no lens displacement or thrombosis
whyNot.E: **thrombosis alone**; does not cause lens dislocation or intellectual disability

why: **Ectopia lentis + thromboembolism + intellectual disability** with unaffected parents = autosomal recessive homocystinuria.

stem: A 14-year-old girl has a red, scaly rash on her face and forearms that appears after sun exposure, and she has had intermittent unsteady gait. Her diet is balanced. Urine amino acid screen shows excess neutral amino acids with no glucose or phosphate loss, and serum tryptophan is low.
oneliner: 14F + photosensitive rash + intermittent ataxia + balanced diet + urine neutral amino acids + low tryptophan → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **urine amino acids are normal**, and a balanced diet gives no niacin shortfall
whyNot.B: **excess dibasic amino acids (cystine, ornithine, lysine, arginine)** with stones, not neutral ones; no rash
whyNot.C: **flushing and diarrhea** from serotonin; no neutral aminoaciduria
whyNot.E: **glucosuria and phosphaturia** accompany the aminoaciduria; urine shows neither

why: **Neutral aminoaciduria + low tryptophan** with a pellagra-like photosensitive rash despite adequate diet = defective neutral amino acid transport (less niacin made from tryptophan).

stem: A 6-day-old boy, well at birth, has poor feeding, vomiting, and lethargy. Blood gas shows a high anion gap metabolic acidosis, ammonia is elevated, and urine ketones are positive. His older brother died of a similar illness at 8 days of age. There is no unusual urine odor.
oneliner: 6d M + vomiting + lethargy + high-AG acidosis + high ammonia + ketonuria + brother died day 8 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **respiratory alkalosis** with hyperammonemia, not a high anion gap metabolic acidosis
whyNot.B: **normal anion gap** and no hyperammonemia
whyNot.C: **hypoketotic** hypoglycemia; here ketones are positive
whyNot.D: **ammonia usually normal** and a burnt-sugar odor; no odor here

answer: Organic acidemia (e.g., propionic or methylmalonic acidemia)
why: **Neonatal lethargy with severe anion gap acidosis, hyperammonemia and ketonuria**, plus an early sibling death = organic acidemia.

stem: A 5-month-old girl has seizures, hypotonia, and poor head control. She has a scaly red rash around the mouth and in the diaper area, thinning scalp hair, and failed her hearing screen. pH is 7.28, bicarbonate 15 mEq/L, lactate 4.5 mmol/L (normal 0.5-2.2). Urine organic acids show raised 3-hydroxyisovalerate and methylcitrate.
oneliner: 5mo F + seizures + hypotonia + periorificial rash + alopecia + deafness + lactic acidosis + organic aciduria → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **burnt-sugar odor and branched-chain ketoacids**; no alopecia or rash
whyNot.C: **no acidosis**; musty odor, fair skin and eczema rather than alopecia and hearing loss
whyNot.D: **zinc deficiency causes rash and alopecia with diarrhea** but no organic aciduria or lactic acidosis
whyNot.E: **lens dislocation and thrombosis**, with no organic aciduria

answer: Multiple carboxylase deficiency (biotinidase or holocarboxylase synthetase deficiency)
why: **Seizures + alopecia + rash + deafness with lactic acidosis and organic aciduria** = failure of the biotin-dependent carboxylases.

stem: A 6-month-old girl develops vomiting and lethargy two days after starting a high-protein formula. Labs: ammonia 280 µmol/L (normal <50), pH 7.48, BUN 3 mg/dL. Plasma citrulline is low, and urine orotic acid is markedly elevated.
oneliner: 6mo F + vomiting + lethargy after protein load + high ammonia + low BUN + low citrulline + high urine orotic acid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **urine orotic acid is low**, not high
whyNot.C: **plasma citrulline is very high**, here it is low
whyNot.D: **argininosuccinate in urine and moderately high citrulline**; citrulline is low here
whyNot.E: **high arginine with spastic diplegia**, and ammonia is only mildly raised

why: **Hyperammonemia + low citrulline + high orotic acid**: carbamoyl phosphate piles up behind the OTC block and spills into pyrimidine synthesis.

stem: A 4-day-old boy is lethargic and vomiting, with ammonia 300 µmol/L. Urine amino acid analysis shows large amounts of argininosuccinic acid.
oneliner: 4d M + lethargy + vomiting + high ammonia + urine argininosuccinate → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **block is one step earlier**, so citrulline accumulates and argininosuccinate is not made
whyNot.B: **block comes before argininosuccinate is formed**; urine would show orotic acid, not argininosuccinate
whyNot.C: **last step of the cycle**; arginine accumulates, not argininosuccinate
whyNot.E: **first-step block**; no urea cycle intermediates build up, so no argininosuccinate

why: **Argininosuccinate in urine** with hyperammonemia = block at argininosuccinate lyase.

stem: A 3-year-old boy with intellectual disability and dystonia repeatedly bites his lips and fingers, causing tissue loss. Serum uric acid is markedly elevated.
oneliner: 3M + intellectual disability + dystonia + biting lips/fingers + high uric acid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **adult joint disease**; does not cause intellectual disability or self-mutilation
whyNot.C: **severe immunodeficiency** with low uric acid, not high
whyNot.D: **low uric acid** and xanthine stones
whyNot.E: **no hyperuricemia**; self-biting is not a typical feature

why: **Self-mutilation + intellectual disability + hyperuricemia** in a boy = X-linked HGPRT deficiency (purine salvage defect).

stem: A 9-day-old exclusively breastfed girl is jaundiced and vomits after feeds. She is afebrile with hepatomegaly. Urine is positive for reducing substances but negative on a glucose-oxidase dipstick.
oneliner: 9d F + breastfed + jaundice + vomiting + hepatomegaly + urine reducing substance positive, glucose oxidase negative → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **symptoms start after fructose or sucrose is introduced**; she is on breast milk only
whyNot.B: **conjugated jaundice with pale stools**; no reducing substances in urine
whyNot.C: **fever or instability**; she is afebrile and the urine test points to a sugar
whyNot.D: **diarrhea and gas** without jaundice or hepatomegaly

why: **Reducing substance in urine but glucose-oxidase negative**, with jaundice and hepatomegaly in a milk-fed newborn = galactose in urine.

stem: A 3-month-old girl is brought to the emergency department after 24 hours of vomiting and poor feeding during a viral illness. She is lethargic and tachypneic, and the liver edge is 3 cm below the costal margin. Glucose is 28 mg/dL, pH 7.21, and lactate 7.5 mmol/L; urine ketones are positive. She has not been fed fruit, juice or sucrose. A monitored test later shows that blood glucose rises after galactose but not after glycerol or fructose.
oneliner: 3mo F + fasting during illness + hypoglycemia + lactic acidosis + ketosis + hepatomegaly + glucose rises with galactose, not glycerol or fructose → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **galactose would not raise glucose either**, because the block is the final step (glucose-6-phosphatase)
whyNot.B: **symptoms follow fructose or sucrose intake**; none was given before this attack
whyNot.D: **hypoketotic hypoglycemia without lactic acidosis**; here ketones are positive and lactate is high
whyNot.E: **galactose is poorly tolerated**, but here it safely raises glucose

why: **Fasting hypoglycemia with lactic acidosis; glucose rises with galactose but not glycerol or fructose** = gluconeogenesis blocked above fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase.

stem: A 4-month-old boy has marked hypotonia, a large protruding tongue, and feeding difficulty. Chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly. Glucose, lactate and uric acid are normal.
oneliner: 4mo M + floppy + big tongue + cardiomegaly + normal glucose, lactate and uric acid → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **fasting hypoglycemia, lactic acidosis and hyperuricemia**; all normal here
whyNot.C: **hepatomegaly with hypoglycemia**; no cardiomegaly or macroglossia
whyNot.D: **exercise cramps in young adults**, not infantile hypotonia
whyNot.E: **hepatosplenomegaly progressing to cirrhosis**, not macroglossia with cardiomegaly

answer: Pompe disease (acid maltase deficiency, GSD type II)
why: **Floppy infant + macroglossia + cardiomegaly with normal glucose** = lysosomal acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency.

stem: An 18-month-old boy is found lethargic after a 14-hour fast. Glucose is 32 mg/dL, urine ketones are negative, and free fatty acids are high. Plasma carnitine is low, urine shows long-chain dicarboxylic acids, and the liver is mildly enlarged. His glucose and alertness improve with IV dextrose, and he later does well on a diet with medium-chain triglyceride oil.
oneliner: 18mo M + fasting hypoglycemia + no ketones + low carnitine + dicarboxylic aciduria + hepatomegaly + improves on MCT oil → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **MCT oil is itself a medium-chain substrate** this enzyme cannot oxidize; improvement on MCT argues for a long-chain block
whyNot.B: **very low carnitine without dicarboxylic aciduria**
whyNot.C: **ketones and lactate are high** with hyperuricemia; ketones are absent here
whyNot.E: **ketotic hypoglycemia**; here ketones are negative

why: **Hypoketotic hypoglycemia + dicarboxylic aciduria, improving on MCT oil** = fatty acid beta-oxidation block in the long-chain step.

stem: A 21-year-old woman of Japanese descent develops facial flushing and palpitations within minutes of a single glass of wine. She takes no medications.
oneliner: 21F + Japanese + flushing + palpitations after one glass of wine + no meds → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **requires disulfiram or a similar drug**; she takes none
whyNot.C: **flushing and diarrhea unrelated to alcohol**
whyNot.D: **a first glass of wine** does not imply dependence; reaction is immediate and physical
whyNot.E: **ethanol would persist** with intoxication rather than flushing from acetaldehyde

why: **East Asian ancestry + flushing after minimal alcohol** = acetaldehyde accumulation from mutant ALDH2.

stem: A 30-year-old woman who was well before surgery remains apneic and flaccid 2 hours after succinylcholine for an appendectomy. Temperature is normal and there is no muscle rigidity.
oneliner: 30F + well before surgery + paralysed 2 h after succinylcholine + normal temp + no rigidity → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **hyperthermia and muscle rigidity**; temperature is normal and muscles flaccid
whyNot.B: **preexisting fluctuating weakness** with ptosis; she was well before surgery
whyNot.C: **fever and lead-pipe rigidity** after dopamine blockers
whyNot.D: **preexisting proximal weakness with autonomic signs**; she was well before surgery

why: **Prolonged flaccid paralysis after succinylcholine** without fever or rigidity = the drug is not being hydrolyzed by plasma cholinesterase.

stem: A 3-day-old term girl, feeding well, looks mildly yellow to the chest. She was not jaundiced in the first 24 hours. Total bilirubin is 8 mg/dL (direct 0.5), hemoglobin 17 g/dL, reticulocytes normal, and the Coombs test is negative. The yellow color fades by day 8.
oneliner: 3d F + jaundice after day 1 + indirect bilirubin 8 + normal Hb, Coombs negative + gone by day 8 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **severe, persistent unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia**; this resolves in days
whyNot.B: **hemolysis with low hemoglobin and raised reticulocytes**; both normal
whyNot.D: **mild jaundice in adolescence or adulthood** with stress or fasting
whyNot.E: **conjugated bilirubin and pale stools**; direct fraction is normal here

why: **Unconjugated jaundice after day 1, no hemolysis, resolving within days** = immature UGT and bilirubin load in a healthy newborn.

stem: A 14-month-old girl has coarse facial features, gingival hyperplasia, stiff joints, and developmental delay. X-rays show dysostosis multiplex. Plasma levels of lysosomal enzymes are markedly raised, and urine glycosaminoglycans are normal.
oneliner: 14mo F + coarse face + gingival hyperplasia + stiff joints + delay + dysostosis multiplex + high plasma lysosomal enzymes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **iduronidase is deficient**, and urine glycosaminoglycans are raised
whyNot.B: **hepatosplenomegaly and bone crises** without coarse facies
whyNot.C: **cherry-red macula and hyperacusis**, no coarse features or dysostosis
whyNot.E: **X-linked, so girls are not affected**, and urine glycosaminoglycans are high

why: **Coarse facies + dysostosis multiplex + high plasma lysosomal enzymes, normal urine GAGs** = no mannose-6-phosphate tag, so enzymes leak out instead of reaching lysosomes.

stem: A 3-year-old boy has progressively coarse facial features, thick body hair, an enlarged liver, stiff joints and developmental delay. X-rays show dysostosis multiplex, and urine glycosaminoglycans are markedly increased.
oneliner: 3M + progressive coarse face + hirsutism + hepatomegaly + stiff joints + delay + dysostosis + high urine GAGs → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **urine glycosaminoglycans are normal** and plasma lysosomal enzymes are high
whyNot.C: **hepatosplenomegaly and bone pain** without coarse facies or high urine GAGs

stem: A 20-month-old girl has poor growth, polyuria and bowed legs, and she squints in bright light. Labs show low phosphate, glucosuria with normal serum glucose, and generalized aminoaciduria. Slit-lamp exam shows crystals in the cornea.

stem: A 15-year-old girl is seen for 2 days of severe headache and vomiting, followed by a focal seizure of the right arm. She now has right arm weakness and cannot see to the right. why: **Stroke-like episode not in one arterial territory + lactic acidosis + maternal inheritance** = MELAS.
